claim: Mammalian cardiomyocytes become post-mitotic shortly after birth.
source: Mammalian cardiomyocytes become post-mitotic shortly after birth.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 1996 and Soonpaa et al., 1996 in the Introduction section

claim: Cardiomyocyte centrosome integrity is lost shortly after birth.
source: Here, we show that cardiomyocyte centrosome integrity is lost shortly after birth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing centriole splitting in postnatal cardiomyocytes

claim: Centrosome proteins relocalize to the nuclear envelope in postnatal cardiomyocytes.
source: This is coupled with relocalization of various centrosome proteins to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing PCM1, Pericentrin, and Cdk5Rap2 at the nuclear envelope

claim: Postnatal cardiomyocytes are unable to undergo ciliogenesis.
source: Consequently, postnatal cardiomyocytes are unable to undergo ciliogenesis and the nuclear envelope adopts the function as cellular microtubule organizing center.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing less than 1% of postnatal cardiomyocytes form primary cilia

claim: The nuclear envelope adopts the function as cellular microtubule organizing center in postnatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Consequently, postnatal cardiomyocytes are unable to undergo ciliogenesis and the nuclear envelope adopts the function as cellular microtubule organizing center.
evidence: Supported by microtubule regrowth assays showing microtubules emanate from the nuclear envelope in P3 cardiomyocytes

claim: Loss of centrosome integrity is associated with cardiomyocyte G0/G1 cell cycle arrest.
source: Loss of centrosome integrity is associated with, and can promote, cardiomyocyte G0/G1 cell cycle arrest suggesting that centrosome disassembly is developmentally utilized to achieve the post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by data showing P3 cardiomyocytes with split centrioles have lower proliferative potential than those with paired centrioles

claim: Loss of centrosome integrity can promote cardiomyocyte G0/G1 cell cycle arrest.
source: Loss of centrosome integrity is associated with, and can promote, cardiomyocyte G0/G1 cell cycle arrest suggesting that centrosome disassembly is developmentally utilized to achieve the post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by siRNA knockdown of Pcnt and overexpression of dominant negative Pericentrin reducing cardiomyocyte proliferative potential

claim: Centrosome disassembly is developmentally utilized to achieve the post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
source: Loss of centrosome integrity is associated with, and can promote, cardiomyocyte G0/G1 cell cycle arrest suggesting that centrosome disassembly is developmentally utilized to achieve the post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between centrosome disassembly and cell cycle arrest during development

claim: Adult cardiomyocytes of zebrafish maintain centrosome integrity.
source: Adult cardiomyocytes of zebrafish and newt, which are able to proliferate, maintain centrosome integrity.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing paired centrioles in adult zebrafish cardiomyocytes

claim: Adult cardiomyocytes of newt maintain centrosome integrity.
source: Adult cardiomyocytes of zebrafish and newt, which are able to proliferate, maintain centrosome integrity.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing paired centrioles in adult newt cardiomyocytes

claim: The adult mammalian heart is considered to be a post-mitotic organ.
source: The adult mammalian heart is considered to be a post-mitotic organ, as mammalian cardiomyocytes lose their ability to proliferate shortly after birth (Li et al., 1996; Soonpaa et al., 1996; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Mammalian cardiomyocytes lose their ability to proliferate shortly after birth.
source: The adult mammalian heart is considered to be a post-mitotic organ, as mammalian cardiomyocytes lose their ability to proliferate shortly after birth (Li et al., 1996; Soonpaa et al., 1996; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 1996; Soonpaa et al., 1996; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013

claim: The adult mammalian heart has limited regenerative capacity.
source: This is supported by the limited regenerative capacity of the adult mammalian heart (Senyo et al., 2014) and the fact that primary adult cardiomyocyte-born tumors are extremely rare, if they exist at all (Dell'Amore et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Senyo et al., 2014

claim: Primary adult cardiomyocyte-born tumors are extremely rare, if they exist at all.
source: This is supported by the limited regenerative capacity of the adult mammalian heart (Senyo et al., 2014) and the fact that primary adult cardiomyocyte-born tumors are extremely rare, if they exist at all (Dell'Amore et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dell'Amore et al., 2011

claim: Zebrafish can regenerate their heart through cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: In contrast to mammals, adult newts and zebrafish can regenerate their heart through cardiomyocyte proliferation (Poss et al., 2002; Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poss et al., 2002 and Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2003

claim: Newts can regenerate their heart through cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: In contrast to mammals, adult newts and zebrafish can regenerate their heart through cardiomyocyte proliferation (Poss et al., 2002; Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poss et al., 2002 and Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2003

claim: Cell cycle promoting factors (e.g., Cyclins) are downregulated around birth in cardiomyocytes.
source: However, besides the fact that cell cycle promoting factors (e.g., Cyclins) are downregulated around birth, while cell cycle inhibitors (e.g., Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors) are induced (Ikenishi et al., 2012), little is known about the mechanisms that induce cell cycle exit or establish the post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes (van Amerongen and Engel, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ikenishi et al., 2012

claim: Cell cycle inhibitors (e.g., Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors) are induced around birth in cardiomyocytes.
source: However, besides the fact that cell cycle promoting factors (e.g., Cyclins) are downregulated around birth, while cell cycle inhibitors (e.g., Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors) are induced (Ikenishi et al., 2012), little is known about the mechanisms that induce cell cycle exit or establish the post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes (van Amerongen and Engel, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ikenishi et al., 2012

claim: The centrosome consists of a pair of tubulin-based structures called centrioles.
source: It consists of a pair of tubulin-based structures, called centrioles, encased in a dense, non-membranous, multi-protein cloud called the pericentriolar matrix (PCM), which is further surrounded by a dispersed array of proteins termed centriolar satellites (Bettencourt-Dias, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bettencourt-Dias, 2013 and established scientific knowledge

claim: Centrioles are encased in a pericentriolar matrix (PCM).
source: It consists of a pair of tubulin-based structures, called centrioles, encased in a dense, non-membranous, multi-protein cloud called the pericentriolar matrix (PCM), which is further surrounded by a dispersed array of proteins termed centriolar satellites (Bettencourt-Dias, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bettencourt-Dias, 2013 and established scientific knowledge

claim: The centrosome is known as the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) of the cell.
source: Traditionally, the centrosome is known as the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) of the cell, and is required for primary cilium formation (Kim and Dynlacht, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Dynlacht, 2013 and established scientific knowledge

claim: The centrosome is required for primary cilium formation.
source: Traditionally, the centrosome is known as the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) of the cell, and is required for primary cilium formation (Kim and Dynlacht, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Dynlacht, 2013

claim: The centrosome has emerged as a critical signaling hub for the cell cycle regulatory machinery.
source: Recently, the centrosome has emerged as a critical signaling hub for the cell cycle regulatory machinery (Doxsey et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doxsey et al., 2005

claim: Centrosome localization of Cyclin E and Cyclin A is required for G1/S cell cycle progression.
source: For instance, centrosome localization of Cyclin E and Cyclin A is required for G1/S cell cycle progression (Pascreau et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pascreau et al., 2011

claim: A functional centrosome is required for proliferative potential in mammalian cell-types.
source: Consistent with this role, increasing evidence supports the requirement of a functional centrosome for proliferative potential in mammalian cell-types (Doxsey et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doxsey et al., 2005

claim: Cells undergo G0/G1 arrest when centrosomes are removed via laser ablation.
source: For instance, cells undergo G0/G1 arrest when (i) centrosomes are removed via laser ablation, (ii) centrosome integrity is disrupted via knockdown of centrosome proteins, or (iii) centriole biogenesis is blocked via a chemical inhibitor (Hinchcliffe et al., 2001; Khodjakov and Rieder, 2001; Srsen et al., 2006; Mikule et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hinchcliffe et al., 2001 and Khodjakov and Rieder, 2001

claim: Cells undergo G0/G1 arrest when centrosome integrity is disrupted via knockdown of centrosome proteins.
source: For instance, cells undergo G0/G1 arrest when (i) centrosomes are removed via laser ablation, (ii) centrosome integrity is disrupted via knockdown of centrosome proteins, or (iii) centriole biogenesis is blocked via a chemical inhibitor (Hinchcliffe et al., 2001; Khodjakov and Rieder, 2001; Srsen et al., 2006; Mikule et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Srsen et al., 2006 and Mikule et al., 2007

claim: Cells undergo G0/G1 arrest when centriole biogenesis is blocked via a chemical inhibitor.
source: For instance, cells undergo G0/G1 arrest when (i) centrosomes are removed via laser ablation, (ii) centrosome integrity is disrupted via knockdown of centrosome proteins, or (iii) centriole biogenesis is blocked via a chemical inhibitor (Hinchcliffe et al., 2001; Khodjakov and Rieder, 2001; Srsen et al., 2006; Mikule et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2015

claim: A normal diploid cell in G0/G1-phase contains one centrosome with two paired centrioles.
source: A normal diploid cell in G0/G1-phase contains one centrosome with two paired centrioles.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of cell cycle and centrosome biology

claim: During S-phase the centrosome duplicates whereby the two parental centrioles form daughter centrioles.
source: During S-phase the centrosome duplicates whereby the two parental centrioles form daughter centrioles.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of centrosome duplication

claim: Around the transition from G2-phase to mitosis, parental centrioles 'split' (loss of cohesion) resulting in two separated centrosomes.
source: Around the transition from G2-phase to mitosis, parental centrioles 'split' (loss of cohesion) resulting in two separated centrosomes that become part of the spindle poles during mitosis (Doxsey et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doxsey et al., 2005 and established knowledge

claim: When centrosome integrity is compromised during G0/G1-phase, centrioles can lose cohesion adopting a premature 'split' configuration.
source: When centrosome integrity is compromised during G0/G1-phase, centrioles can lose cohesion (i.e., become unpaired) adopting a premature 'split' configuration, defined as a distance > 2 µm between centrioles (Graser et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graser et al., 2007

claim: Premature centriole split is defined as a distance > 2 µm between centrioles.
source: When centrosome integrity is compromised during G0/G1-phase, centrioles can lose cohesion (i.e., become unpaired) adopting a premature 'split' configuration, defined as a distance > 2 µm between centrioles (Graser et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graser et al., 2007

claim: Centrioles were in a typical paired configuration in the majority of cultured cardiomyocytes isolated from embryonic day (E) 15, E18, and postnatal day (P) 0 rat hearts.
source: Centrioles were observed to be in a typical paired configuration in the majority of cultured cardiomyocytes isolated from embryonic day (E) 15, E18, and postnatal day (P) 0 rat hearts (Figure 1A,B) as well as in cardiomyocytes from E15 and P0 rat heart sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Centrioles were split in the vast majority of P3 and P5 cardiomyocytes in vitro.
source: In contrast, shortly after birth, centrioles were split in the vast majority of P3 and P5 cardiomyocytes in vitro (Figure 1A,B) and in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Centrioles were split in the vast majority of P3 and P5 cardiomyocytes in vivo.
source: In contrast, shortly after birth, centrioles were split in the vast majority of P3 and P5 cardiomyocytes in vitro (Figure 1A,B) and in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Each γ-tubulin signal represents a single centriole in rat cardiomyocytes.
source: Analysis of mother and daughter centriole markers (Odf2 and Centrobin, respectively) in isolated rat cardiomyocytes verified that each γ-tubulin signal represented a single centriole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing Odf2 and Centrobin markers

claim: The majority of non-myocytes in the heart showed a typical paired-centriole configuration at all examined developmental stages.
source: At all examined developmental stages, non-myocytes showed a typical paired-centriole configuration indicating that the split-centriole phenotype was cardiomyocyte-specific (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The split-centriole phenotype is cardiomyocyte-specific.
source: At all examined developmental stages, non-myocytes showed a typical paired-centriole configuration indicating that the split-centriole phenotype was cardiomyocyte-specific (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that non-myocytes maintain paired centrioles while cardiomyocytes develop split centrioles

claim: Centriole cohesion is lost in mammalian cardiomyocytes shortly after birth.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that centriole cohesion, and thus centrosome integrity, is lost in mammalian cardiomyocytes shortly after birth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing centriole splitting in postnatal cardiomyocytes

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 are required for centriole-cohesion.
source: The PCM proteins Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 have previously been shown to be required for centriole-cohesion (Graser et al., 2007; Matsuo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graser et al., 2007 and Matsuo et al., 2010

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 localized to the centrosome in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Consistent with this function, both PCM proteins localized to the centrosome in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 were localized to the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: In contrast, both proteins were localized to the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: Remnants of Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 could be observed at the centriole in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Although remnants of Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 could be observed at the centriole in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), their presence was significantly reduced when centrioles were split (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,D,E

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 presence at centrioles was significantly reduced when centrioles were split.
source: Although remnants of Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 could be observed at the centriole in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), their presence was significantly reduced when centrioles were split (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Pcnt siRNA-mediated knockdown in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in an increase of split-centrioles.
source: Pcnt siRNA-mediated knockdown in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in an increase of split-centrioles (Figure 1F,G), confirming that Pericentrin is required for centriole-cohesion in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G

claim: Pericentrin is required for centriole-cohesion in cardiomyocytes.
source: Pcnt siRNA-mediated knockdown in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in an increase of split-centrioles (Figure 1F,G), confirming that Pericentrin is required for centriole-cohesion in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pcnt knockdown increases split centrioles

claim: The centriole-associated proteins CEP135, Odf2, and Centrobin were not observed at the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: In contrast to PCM proteins, the centriole-associated proteins CEP135, Odf2, and Centrobin were not observed at the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Loss of centriole cohesion is accompanied by redistribution of centrosome proteins to the nuclear envelope.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that loss of centriole cohesion is accompanied by redistribution of centrosome proteins to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PCM proteins relocalize to the nuclear envelope when centrioles split

claim: Centrosome localization of Pericentrin is dependent on the centriole satellite protein PCM1.
source: Centrosome localization of Pericentrin is dependent on the centriole satellite protein PCM1 (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Barenz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dammermann and Merdes, 2002 and Barenz et al., 2011

claim: PCM1 localized at the centrosome in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Consistent with this, PCM1 localized at the centrosome and the nuclear envelope in E15- and P3-isolated cardiomyocytes, respectively (Figure 1C,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,H

claim: PCM1 localized at the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Consistent with this, PCM1 localized at the centrosome and the nuclear envelope in E15- and P3-isolated cardiomyocytes, respectively (Figure 1C,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,H

claim: Nuclear envelope localization of PCM1 occurred by P0, prior to that of Pericentrin.
source: Further, nuclear envelope localization of PCM1 occurred by P0 (Figure 1H), prior to that of Pericentrin (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H and 1D

claim: In cardiomyocytes, PCM1 is required for the localization of Pericentrin to the centrosome.
source: These data suggest that in cardiomyocytes, PCM1 is also required for the localization of Pericentrin to the centrosome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PCM1 relocalizes before Pericentrin and the known dependency of Pericentrin on PCM1

claim: Pericentrin B-GFP localized to centrioles in non-myocytes.
source: Pericentrin B-GFP localized to centrioles in non-myocytes as well as E15-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Pericentrin B-GFP localized to centrioles in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Pericentrin B-GFP localized to centrioles in non-myocytes as well as E15-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Pericentrin B-GFP did not localize to the centrioles in the vast majority of P0- and P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: In contrast, Pericentrin B-GFP did not localize to the centrioles in the vast majority of P0- and P3-isolated cardiomyocytes but rather created cellular aggregates which were not observed in E15 cardiomyocytes or non-myocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: The machinery required for centrosome integrity is lost in postnatal cardiomyocytes.
source: These data indicate that the machinery required for centrosome integrity is lost in postnatal cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that overexpressed Pericentrin B-GFP cannot localize to centrioles in postnatal cardiomyocytes

claim: Long-term culturing of E15-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in PCM1 and Pericentrin relocalization to the nuclear envelope.
source: Long-term culturing of E15-isolated and P0-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in PCM1 and Pericentrin relocalization to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1I) and loss of paired-centrioles (Figure 1J), respectively.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Long-term culturing of P0-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in loss of paired-centrioles.
source: Long-term culturing of E15-isolated and P0-isolated cardiomyocytes resulted in PCM1 and Pericentrin relocalization to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1I) and loss of paired-centrioles (Figure 1J), respectively.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1J

claim: Mouse iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes had split-centrioles.
source: Further, mouse iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes had split-centrioles and the centrosome proteins PCM1 and Pericentrin localized to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: In mouse iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, the centrosome proteins PCM1 and Pericentrin localized to the nuclear envelope.
source: Further, mouse iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes had split-centrioles and the centrosome proteins PCM1 and Pericentrin localized to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Loss of centrosome integrity begins during fetal development and progresses in a cell autonomous manner.
source: These results indicate that loss of centrosome integrity begins during fetal development and progresses in a cell autonomous manner.
evidence: Inferred from long-term culture experiments showing centrosome disassembly occurs in isolated cardiomyocytes

claim: Pcnt is alternatively spliced, resulting in two isoforms: Pericentrin B and Pericentrin S.
source: Previously, it has been demonstrated that Pcnt is alternatively spliced (Miyoshi et al., 2006), resulting in two isoforms; Pericentrin B which resembles the human Pericentrin Kendrin, and Pericentrin S, which lacks an N-terminus region.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyoshi et al., 2006

claim: Pericentrin B is ubiquitously expressed at all developmental stages.
source: Pericentrin B is ubiquitously expressed at all developmental stages.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyoshi et al., 2006 in the preceding sentence

claim: Expression of Pericentrin S starts late in fetal development and is specific for adult heart and skeletal muscle.
source: In contrast, expression of Pericentrin S starts late in fetal development and was found to be specific for adult heart and skeletal muscle (Miyoshi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyoshi et al., 2006

claim: Pcnt S expression appears shortly before birth in the heart.
source: RT-PCR analysis revealed the appearance of Pcnt S expression shortly before birth in the heart (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1K

claim: Pericentrin S, and not Pericentrin B, was the predominant Pericentrin isoform at the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Antibodies specific for the Pericentrin B isoform indicated that Pericentrin S, and not Pericentrin B, was the predominant Pericentrin isoform at the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1L

claim: Pcnt is alternatively spliced during perinatal heart development and this change is related to its relocalization to the nuclear envelope.
source: These results indicate that Pcnt is alternatively spliced during perinatal heart development and this change is related to its relocalization to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pericentrin S expression coincides with nuclear envelope localization

claim: Nearly all cell-types studied to date are capable of forming a primary cilium when arrested in G0/G1-phase.
source: Nearly all cell-types studied to date are capable of forming a primary cilium when arrested in G0/G1-phase (Bowser and Wheatley, 2000, Nigg and Stearns, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bowser and Wheatley, 2000 and Nigg and Stearns, 2011

claim: Cardiomyocytes are arrested shortly after birth in G0/G1 phase.
source: This suggests that cardiomyocytes, which are arrested shortly after birth in G0/G1 phase (Takeuchi, 2014), should be capable of ciliogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Takeuchi, 2014

claim: PCM1 is required for ciliogenesis.
source: Yet, given that PCM1, which is required for ciliogenesis (Kim et al., 2008), is lost from the centrosome during development, we speculated that ciliogenesis is suppressed in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2008

claim: Induction of ciliogenesis via serum starvation resulted in the formation of a primary cilium in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Induction of ciliogenesis via serum starvation resulted in the formation of a primary cilium in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes and non-myocytes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The frequency of cardiomyocytes capable of ciliogenesis decreased with heart development.
source: However, the frequency of cardiomyocytes capable of ciliogenesis decreased with heart development (Figure 2B) with less than 1% of isolated postnatal cardiomyocytes, which were arrested in G1/G0 as confirmed by lack of Ki67 expression and FACS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), forming a primary cilium.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Less than 1% of isolated postnatal cardiomyocytes form a primary cilium.
source: However, the frequency of cardiomyocytes capable of ciliogenesis decreased with heart development (Figure 2B) with less than 1% of isolated postnatal cardiomyocytes, which were arrested in G1/G0 as confirmed by lack of Ki67 expression and FACS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), forming a primary cilium.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B

claim: No postnatal binucleated cardiomyocytes were observed to be capable of ciliogenesis.
source: Further, no postnatal binucleated cardiomyocytes were observed to be capable of ciliogenesis (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The frequency of cardiac non-myocytes capable of ciliogenesis was high at all developmental stages investigated.
source: In contrast to cardiomyocytes, the frequency of cardiac non-myocytes capable of ciliogenesis was high at all developmental stages investigated (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 are required for the centrosome to function as the cellular MTOC.
source: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 are required for the centrosome to function as the cellular MTOC (Takahashi et al., 2002; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2002 and Choi et al., 2010

claim: Microtubules predominantly emanate from the centrosome in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: In accordance with this hypothesis, microtubules were found to predominantly emanate from the centrosome in E15-isolated cardiomyocytes as also observed in non-myocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In P3-isolated cardiomyocytes microtubules predominantly emanate from the nuclear envelope.
source: In contrast, in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes microtubules were found to predominantly emanate from the nuclear envelope (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Microtubules do not emanate from centrioles in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: The local shift of the MTOC during development was confirmed by a MTOC-regrowth assay (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F), which further demonstrated that microtubules do not emanate from centrioles in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by MTOC regrowth assay data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Pericentrin is required for a functional MTOC at the nuclear envelope in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Finally, siRNA-mediated knockdown of Pcnt in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes demonstrated that Pericentrin is required for a functional MTOC at the nuclear envelope (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by siRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Traditional centrosome functions of ciliogenesis and microtubule organization are lost in postnatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that, in addition to centrosome integrity, centrosome function is progressively compromised in cardiomyocytes during development.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that postnatal cardiomyocytes cannot form cilia and have nuclear envelope-based MTOC

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferative potential decreased with neonatal development.
source: Cardiomyocyte proliferative potential decreased with neonatal development (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3A

claim: P3-isolated cardiomyocytes with paired-centrioles exhibited greater proliferative potential than those with split centrioles.
source: Moreover, P3-isolated cardiomyocytes with paired-centrioles exhibited greater proliferative potential than those with split centrioles (Figure 3B,C) at a frequency similar to that of E15- and P0-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 3A,C)—of which the vast majority have paired-centrioles (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: Cardiac non-myocyte proliferative potential did not decrease during neonatal development.
source: In contrast, cardiac non-myocyte proliferative potential, as well as the percentage of non-myocytes with paired centrioles, did not decrease during neonatal development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The percentage of non-myocytes with paired centrioles did not decrease during neonatal development.
source: In contrast, cardiac non-myocyte proliferative potential, as well as the percentage of non-myocytes with paired centrioles, did not decrease during neonatal development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by centriole configuration data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: RFP-PeriCT localizes to the centrioles in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis confirmed that RFP-PeriCT localizes to the centrioles in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Disruption of centrosome integrity by Pcnt siRNA-mediated knockdown suppressed P0-isolated cardiomyocyte proliferative potential.
source: Both methods used to disrupt centrosome integrity suppressed P0-isolated cardiomyocyte proliferative potential (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Disruption of centrosome integrity by overexpression of RFP-PeriCT suppressed P0-isolated cardiomyocyte proliferative potential.
source: Both methods used to disrupt centrosome integrity suppressed P0-isolated cardiomyocyte proliferative potential (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Loss of centrosome integrity promotes G0/G1 cell cycle arrest in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that loss of centrosome integrity promotes G0/G1 cell cycle arrest in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that disrupting centrosome integrity reduces cardiomyocyte proliferative potential

claim: Disruption of centrosome integrity promotes p38MAP kinase (p38)-mediated G1/S cell cycle arrest.
source: Disruption of centrosome integrity promotes p38MAP kinase (p38)-mediated G1/S cell cycle arrest (Mikule et al., 2007; Pascreau et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mikule et al., 2007 and Pascreau et al., 2011

claim: p38 inhibition allows postnatal cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Previously, it has been demonstrated that p38 inhibition (p38i) allows postnatal cardiomyocyte proliferation (Engel et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engel et al., 2005

claim: p38i enhanced the proliferative potential of P3-isolated cardiomyocytes with split-centrioles.
source: p38i enhanced the proliferative potential of P3-isolated cardiomyocytes with split-centrioles (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Suppression of the p38-mediated stress-activated pathway can promote cell cycle progression in cardiomyocytes that lack centriole-cohesion.
source: These results indicate that suppression of the p38-mediated stress-activated pathway can promote cell cycle progression in cardiomyocytes that lack centriole-cohesion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p38i enhances proliferation in cardiomyocytes with split centrioles

claim: A bipolar mitotic spindle is required for high fidelity chromosome segregation.
source: A bipolar mitotic spindle is required for high fidelity chromosome segregation (Pihan, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pihan, 2013

claim: P0- and P3-isolated cardiomyocytes exhibited a typical metaphase consisting of two γ-tubulin foci in response to serum stimulation.
source: In response to serum stimulation, P0- and P3-isolated cardiomyocytes exhibited a typical metaphase consisting of two γ-tubulin foci (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G,H

claim: p38i had no effect on the number of γ-tubulin foci in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes during metaphase.
source: p38i had no effect on the number of γ-tubulin foci in P0-isolated cardiomyocytes during metaphase (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3H

claim: p38i resulted in a significant increase in metaphases containing multiple γ-tubulin foci in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes.
source: In contrast, p38i resulted in a significant increase in metaphases containing multiple γ-tubulin foci in P3-isolated cardiomyocytes (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative data shown in Figure 3G,H

claim: Adult-isolated cardiomyocytes induced to re-enter the cell cycle by p38i + FGF1 exhibited multiple γ-tubulin foci during metaphase.
source: Similarly, adult-isolated cardiomyocytes induced to re-enter the cell cycle by p38i + FGF1 also exhibited multiple γ-tubulin foci during metaphase (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3I

claim: Over-riding cell cycle arrest in cardiomyocytes results in multiple spindle poles.
source: These data indicate that over-riding cell cycle arrest in cardiomyocytes results in multiple spindle poles.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p38i treatment leads to multiple γ-tubulin foci in metaphase

claim: Paired centrioles could readily be identified in adult newt cardiomyocyte nuclei.
source: Paired centrioles could readily be identified in adult newt and zebrafish cardiomyocyte nuclei (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Paired centrioles could readily be identified in adult zebrafish cardiomyocyte nuclei.
source: Paired centrioles could readily be identified in adult newt and zebrafish cardiomyocyte nuclei (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The frequency of newt cardiomyocyte nuclei with intact centrosomes was similar to that of non-myocyte nuclei.
source: Further, the frequency of newt and zebrafish cardiomyocyte nuclei with intact centrosomes was similar to that of non-myocyte nuclei (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The frequency of zebrafish cardiomyocyte nuclei with intact centrosomes was similar to that of non-myocyte nuclei.
source: Further, the frequency of newt and zebrafish cardiomyocyte nuclei with intact centrosomes was similar to that of non-myocyte nuclei (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Centrosomes in zebrafish cardiomyocytes are functional.
source: In addition, MTOC-regrowth assays demonstrated that centrosomes in zebrafish and newt cardiomyocytes are functional (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by MTOC regrowth assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Centrosomes in newt cardiomyocytes are functional.
source: In addition, MTOC-regrowth assays demonstrated that centrosomes in zebrafish and newt cardiomyocytes are functional (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by MTOC regrowth assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Newt cardiomyocytes maintain centrosome integrity throughout adulthood.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that, unlike mammalian cardiomyocytes, newt and zebrafish cardiomyocytes maintain centrosome integrity throughout adulthood.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that adult newt cardiomyocytes have paired centrioles and functional centrosomes

claim: Zebrafish cardiomyocytes maintain centrosome integrity throughout adulthood.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that, unlike mammalian cardiomyocytes, newt and zebrafish cardiomyocytes maintain centrosome integrity throughout adulthood.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that adult zebrafish cardiomyocytes have paired centrioles and functional centrosomes

claim: A significantly larger number of RFP-PeriCT RNA-injected zebrafish embryos showed developmental delay at 24 hr post fertilization compared to control embryos.
source: Compared to control embryos (RFP RNA-injected), a significantly larger number of RFP-PeriCT RNA-injected embryos showed developmental delay at 24 hr post fertilization (hpf) and a significantly reduced number of H3P-positive cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: RFP-PeriCT RNA-injected zebrafish embryos had a significantly reduced number of H3P-positive cells compared to control embryos.
source: Compared to control embryos (RFP RNA-injected), a significantly larger number of RFP-PeriCT RNA-injected embryos showed developmental delay at 24 hr post fertilization (hpf) and a significantly reduced number of H3P-positive cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: The majority of RFP-PeriCT DNA-injected zebrafish embryos contained either no clones or few scattered clones.
source: In contrast, the majority of RFP-PeriCT DNA-injected embryos contained either no clones (class I) or few scattered clones (class II), while larger clones (class III and IV) were rarely seen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: Clonal expansion of RFP-PeriCT expressing cells is reduced in zebrafish embryos.
source: This suggests that clonal expansion of RFP-PeriCT expressing cells is reduced, which substantiates the hypothesis that expression of RFP-PeriCT reduces cell proliferative potential.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RFP-PeriCT expressing cells form smaller clones

claim: Zebrafish cells require centrosome integrity for proliferation in vivo.
source: These results suggest that zebrafish cells require centrosome integrity for proliferation in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that disrupting centrosome integrity with RFP-PeriCT reduces proliferation in zebrafish embryos

claim: Centrosome integrity can be developmentally regulated to achieve a post-mitotic state.
source: This body of literature coupled with our results suggests that centrosome integrity can be developmentally regulated to achieve a post-mitotic state.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that centrosome disassembly occurs during cardiomyocyte development and correlates with cell cycle arrest

claim: Centrosome disassembly appears to be a very effective way to achieve a post-mitotic state.
source: Centrosome disassembly appears to be a very effective way to achieve a post-mitotic state.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that centrosome disassembly correlates with and promotes cell cycle arrest

claim: Centrosome disassembly may be a result of cytoskeletal reorganization in response to increased hemodynamic stress.
source: Effective cardiomyocyte function in response to increased hemodynamic stress may require a cytoskeletal architecture more conducive to handling postnatal physical stresses (e.g., a nuclear envelope-based MTOC). Thus, centrosome disassembly may be a result of cytoskeletal reorganization.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional significance of centrosome disassembly

claim: Proliferative potential might be sacrificed for postnatal function in cardiomyocytes.
source: In this scenario, proliferative potential might be sacrificed for postnatal function.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the trade-off between proliferation and function

claim: Establishment of a post-mitotic state in both skeletal muscle and cardiomyocytes coincides with MTOC relocalization to the nuclear envelope and centrosome disassembly.
source: However, our results together with others (Tassin et al., 1985; Bugnard et al., 2005; Srsen et al., 2006; Fant et al., 2009; Zaal et al., 2011) challenges this dogma, as establishment of a post-mitotic state in both muscle cell-types coincides with MTOC relocalization to the nuclear envelope and centrosome disassembly.
evidence: Supported by the current study's data and citations to Tassin et al., 1985; Bugnard et al., 2005; Srsen et al., 2006; Fant et al., 2009; Zaal et al., 2011

claim: p38i promotes cardiomyocyte proliferative potential in the absence of a functional centrosome.
source: The observation that p38i promotes cardiomyocyte proliferative potential in the absence of a functional centrosome provides some optimism for heart regeneration via proliferation of endogenous cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing p38i enhances proliferation in cardiomyocytes with split centrioles

claim: An absence of centrosome integrity correlates with multiple spindle poles in cardiomyocytes.
source: However, we observe that an absence of centrosome integrity correlates with multiple spindle poles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing multiple γ-tubulin foci in metaphase when cardiomyocytes with split centrioles are induced to proliferate

claim: Multiple spindle poles are generally resolved into a semi-clustered/pseudo-bipolar conformation, but this process is highly prone to the formation of merotelic spindle-kinetochore attachments.
source: Although multiple spindle poles are generally resolved into a semi-clustered/pseudo-bipolar conformation, this process is nevertheless highly prone to the formation of merotelic spindle-kinetochore attachments, which can promote chromosome missegregation (Ganem et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganem et al., 2009

claim: Postnatal cardiomyocytes induced to proliferate exhibit chromosome segregation abnormalities.
source: Indeed, postnatal cardiomyocytes induced to proliferate exhibit chromosome segregation abnormalities (Engel et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engel et al., 2006

claim: Aneuploidy is generally not well tolerated.
source: While cell viability can exist when aneuploidy is limited (e.g., as seen in Down Syndrome), aneuploidy is generally not well tolerated (Torres et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Torres et al., 2008 and established scientific knowledge

claim: Proliferation of adult cardiomyocytes may not necessarily result in viable daughter cells in the absence of a functional centrosome.
source: Therefore, proliferation of adult cardiomyocytes may not necessarily result in viable daughter cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that cardiomyocytes without functional centrosomes have multiple spindle poles and chromosome segregation abnormalities

claim: Whether a particular manipulation induces aneuploidy may be a critical factor in determining its regenerative therapeutic potential.
source: Thus, in the absence of a functional centrosome, whether a particular manipulation induces aneuploidy, and to what degree, may be a critical factor in determining its regenerative therapeutic potential.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the implications for cardiac regeneration therapy

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 are required for centriole-engagement.
source: Interestingly, in addition to centriole-cohesion, Pericentrin and Cdk5Rap2 are also required for centriole-engagement (Barrera et al., 2010; Lee and Rhee, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrera et al., 2010 and Lee and Rhee, 2012

claim: During S-phase, centrioles are duplicated, with each mother centriole forming a daughter centriole, which remains closely attached (i.e., engaged) until mid-anaphase.
source: During S-phase, centrioles are duplicated, with each mother centriole forming a daughter centriole, which remains closely attached (i.e., engaged) until mid-anaphase (Kuriyama and Borisy, 1981; Sluder, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuriyama and Borisy, 1981 and Sluder, 2013

claim: When mother-daughter centrioles are engaged, only the mother centriole exhibits a strong γ-tubulin signal.
source: When mother-daughter centrioles are engaged, only the mother centriole exhibits a strong γ-tubulin signal (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011

claim: When cells that lack centriole-cohesion enter mitosis, they have an increased likelihood of premature loss of centriole-engagement.
source: Thus, one speculation is that when cells that lack centriole-cohesion enter mitosis, they have an increased likelihood of premature loss of centriole-engagement, thus accounting for the four γ-tubulin signals observed at metaphase.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the mechanism of multiple spindle poles

claim: Induction of mitosis in bi-nucleated cardiomyocytes results in four γ-tubulin signals in metaphase corresponding to four duplicated centrioles.
source: However, it has to be considered that induction of mitosis in bi-nucleated cardiomyocytes, which increasingly appear after birth, results in four γ-tubulin signals in metaphase corresponding to four duplicated centrioles.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about an alternative explanation for multiple spindle poles

claim: The state of cellular differentiation of cardiomyocytes from various species is not evolutionary conserved.
source: Our data demonstrate that the state of cellular differentiation of cardiomyocytes from various species is not evolutionary conserved.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that zebrafish and newt cardiomyocytes maintain centrosome integrity while mammalian cardiomyocytes do not

claim: Factors promoting adult zebrafish cardiomyocyte proliferation might not necessarily induce adult mammalian cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: The fact that adult zebrafish and newt cardiomyocytes maintain their centrosome integrity indicates that factors promoting adult zebrafish cardiomyocyte proliferation might not necessarily induce adult mammalian cardiomyocyte proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that zebrafish and mammalian cardiomyocytes have different centrosome states

claim: Planarians can develop and regenerate in the absence of centrosomes.
source: Recently, it has been shown that planarians can develop and regenerate in the absence of centrosomes (Azimzadeh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Azimzadeh et al., 2012

claim: Planarians express only one single repressive E2F, whereas mammals and zebrafish express several repressive and activating E2Fs.
source: For example, planarians express only one single repressive E2F, whereas mammals and zebrafish express several repressive and activating E2Fs.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of cell cycle regulation in different species

claim: Planarians do not have Cyclin E or Cyclin A homologs.
source: In addition, planarians do not have Cyclin E or Cyclin A homologs.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of planarian cell cycle proteins

claim: CDK2 is expressed at such low levels in planarians that it is considered functionally dead.
source: Further, cyclin-dependent kinase CDK2 (to which Cyclin E/A usually binds) is expressed at such low levels in planarians that it is considered functionally dead (Zhu and Pearson, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu and Pearson, 2013

claim: Planarians lack centrosome-regulated cell cycle factors Cyclin E and Cyclin A.
source: Thus, at least in the case of Cyclin E and Cyclin A, planarians lack centrosome-regulated cell cycle factors.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that planarians lack Cyclin E and Cyclin A, which require centrosome localization in mammals

claim: Centrosome integrity is required for proliferation during zebrafish development.
source: In addition, our data indicate that centrosome integrity is required for proliferation during zebrafish development.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that disrupting centrosome integrity reduces proliferation in zebrafish embryos

claim: plk4 depletion in zebrafish impairs centriolar biogenesis during development and increases premature cell cycle exit resulting in reduced zebrafish size.
source: This is in agreement with the recent observation that plk4 depletion in zebrafish impairs centriolar biogenesis during development and increases premature cell cycle exit (independent of ciliogenesis defects) resulting in reduced zebrafish size (Martin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin et al., 2014

claim: Depletion of stil causes cell cycle defects resulting in impaired development.
source: Other examples of centriole-associated genes whose depletion causes cell cycle defects resulting in impaired development are stil (Pfaff et al., 2007; Vulprecht et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014) and cetn2 (Delaval et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pfaff et al., 2007; Vulprecht et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014

claim: Depletion of cetn2 causes cell cycle defects resulting in impaired development.
source: Other examples of centriole-associated genes whose depletion causes cell cycle defects resulting in impaired development are stil (Pfaff et al., 2007; Vulprecht et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014) and cetn2 (Delaval et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Delaval et al., 2011

claim: Inhibition of mps1 impairs cardiac regeneration in zebrafish after apex resection.
source: For example it has been shown that inhibition of mps1 and plk1, factors implicated in centrosome assembly and maturation (Pike and Fisk, 2011; Joukov et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2014), impairs cardiac regeneration in zebrafish after apex resection (Poss et al., 2002; Jopling et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poss et al., 2002 and Jopling et al., 2010

claim: Inhibition of plk1 impairs cardiac regeneration in zebrafish after apex resection.
source: For example it has been shown that inhibition of mps1 and plk1, factors implicated in centrosome assembly and maturation (Pike and Fisk, 2011; Joukov et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2014), impairs cardiac regeneration in zebrafish after apex resection (Poss et al., 2002; Jopling et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poss et al., 2002 and Jopling et al., 2010

claim: mps1 and plk1 are factors implicated in centrosome assembly and maturation.
source: For example it has been shown that inhibition of mps1 and plk1, factors implicated in centrosome assembly and maturation (Pike and Fisk, 2011; Joukov et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2014), impairs cardiac regeneration in zebrafish after apex resection (Poss et al., 2002; Jopling et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pike and Fisk, 2011; Joukov et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2014

claim: Relocalization of the MTOC disrupts centrosome integrity which, in turn, promotes a post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
source: Taken together, this study suggests that relocalization of the MTOC disrupts centrosome integrity which, in turn, promotes a post-mitotic state in mammalian cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the collective observations that MTOC relocalizes, centrosome integrity is lost, and this promotes cell cycle arrest
